title: How does the JVM find the matching catch block: using per-method exception table in bytecode: and why does a non-thrown try block have essentially ZERO runtime cost?
shortTitle: What is the JVM exception table?
keyPoints: Each method in bytecode has an exception table with entries: start-PC, end-PC, handler-PC, and caught exception type
When an exception is thrown, the JVM looks up the table for a matching entry based on PC range and exception type
The try block is just normal bytecode with ZERO overhead: no extra branches, no push/pop markers
The exception table is metadata, not executable code, so it is only consulted when a throw actually happens
If no matching handler is found, the JVM pops the current frame and repeats in the calling method (stack unwinding)
This design means try-catch is free on the happy path and the cost is only paid when exceptions are actually thrown

s1_definition.oneliner: The JVM uses a per-method exception table in bytecode to find catch blocks, and the try block has zero runtime overhead because the table is metadata only consulted when a throw actually happens.
s1_definition.profdef:
- Each compiled method has an **exception table** in its bytecode: a list of entries `[try-start-PC, try-end-PC, handler-PC, caught-type]`.
- When an exception is thrown, the JVM checks the table for the current method: finds an entry where (1) current PC is between try-start and try-end, and (2) thrown exception IS-A caught-type.
- If found, the JVM jumps to handler-PC (the catch block). If not found, it pops the frame and repeats in the calling method (**stack unwinding**).
- The try block is **just normal bytecode** with no extra instructions. No overhead on the happy path. The exception table is metadata, not executable code.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India does not post a guard at every door just in case. Instead, there is an emergency manual in the office (exception table): "If fire alarm between 9AM and 5PM (try range), go to Exit B (handler)." The manual sits unused during normal operations (zero cost). Only when the alarm rings (exception thrown) does someone consult it.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Method Bytecode:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────┐
  │ PC 0-10: try body (plain code)   │ ← no extra instructions
  │ PC 11:   return                  │
  │ PC 13:   catch IAE handler       │
  │ PC 20:   catch RTE handler       │
  └──────────────────────────────────┘

  Exception Table (metadata):
  ┌──────┬──────┬────────┬──────────────────────┐
  │ from │  to  │ target │ type                  │
  ├──────┼──────┼────────┼──────────────────────┤
  │   0  │  10  │   13   │ IllegalArgumentExc    │
  │   0  │  10  │   20   │ RuntimeException      │
  └──────┴──────┴────────┴──────────────────────┘

  Happy path: table never consulted. ZERO cost.
  Exception thrown: table lookup + stack unwinding.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The JVM uses a per-method exception table in the bytecode to find matching catch blocks. Each entry maps a PC range (try body) to a handler PC (catch block) for a specific exception type. When no exception is thrown, the try body executes as plain bytecode with zero overhead. The exception table is metadata, never consulted on the happy path.

The cost appears only when an exception is actually thrown: fillInStackTrace walks the stack (1 to 5 microseconds), the JVM looks up the exception table (fast, small table), and if no match is found, it pops the frame and repeats in the calling method (stack unwinding). This is why try-catch is free but throwing is expensive.

At National Bank of India, Pankaj wraps every database call in try-catch without worrying about performance on the happy path. The try block adds zero overhead. The exception table is only consulted when the database actually throws, which happens rarely compared to successful operations.

Remember one sentence: try-catch has zero runtime cost on the happy path because the exception table is metadata only consulted when a throw actually happens.
